```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7,
                      fig.height = 4)
set.seed(1)
```

`dust2` runs a system that has already been created, for one set of
parameters or one per group. Running a model for many parameter sets, such
as a grid of values or the draws from a fit, takes some bookkeeping: build
each parameter list, create a system with a group per set, set its state,
and keep each trajectory with the parameters that produced it.

`run_parameter_sets()` and `continue_parameter_sets()` do that, and return
an object with the same structure as the output of `monty_sample()`. The
same tidy functions therefore work on a sensitivity analysis, a fit and a
projection.

```{r setup, message = FALSE}
library(tidyodin)
library(odin2)
library(dust2)
library(monty)
library(ggplot2)
library(MetBrewer)
theme_set(theme_bw())
```

## Sensitivity analysis

### A deterministic model

An SIR model written as a set of ODEs:

```{r}
sir_ode <- odin({
  deriv(S) <- -beta * S * I / N
  deriv(I) <- beta * S * I / N - gamma * I
  deriv(R) <- gamma * I
  initial(S) <- N - I0
  initial(I) <- I0
  initial(R) <- 0
  N <- parameter(1000)
  I0 <- parameter(10)
  beta <- parameter(0.4)
  gamma <- parameter(0.1)
}, quiet = TRUE)
```

To see how the epidemic depends on `beta`, give the values to try as a data
frame, with one row per parameter set and one column per parameter that
varies. Parameters that stay the same in every run go in `fixed`:

```{r}
pars <- data.frame(beta = seq(0.15, 0.5, by = 0.05))
res <- run_parameter_sets(sir_ode, pars, times = 0:100,
                          fixed = list(gamma = 0.1))
res
```

The result looks like a set of samples from `monty`, with each parameter
set as one sample. `tidy_trajectories()` and `tidy_pars()` both identify the
parameter set in `sample`, so the two can be joined to label each trajectory
with its value of `beta`:

```{r}
beta <- dplyr::select(tidy_pars(res), sample, beta = value)
traj <- dplyr::left_join(tidy_trajectories(res), beta, by = "sample")
traj

ggplot(traj, aes(time, value, colour = beta, group = beta)) +
  geom_line() +
  facet_wrap(vars(variable)) +
  scale_colour_met_c("Hokusai2")
```

### A stochastic model

The same model in discrete time with stochastic transitions, also tracking
daily incidence and with a comparison to case data that is used for
fitting below:

```{r}
sir <- odin({
  update(S) <- S - n_SI
  update(I) <- I + n_SI - n_IR
  update(R) <- R + n_IR
  update(incidence) <- incidence + n_SI
  p_SI <- 1 - exp(-beta * I / N * dt)
  p_IR <- 1 - exp(-gamma * dt)
  n_SI <- Binomial(S, p_SI)
  n_IR <- Binomial(I, p_IR)
  initial(S) <- N - I0
  initial(I) <- I0
  initial(R) <- 0
  initial(incidence, zero_every = 1) <- 0
  N <- parameter(1000)
  I0 <- parameter(10)
  beta <- parameter(0.4)
  gamma <- parameter(0.1)
  cases <- data()
  cases ~ Poisson(incidence)
}, quiet = TRUE)
```

Each run of a stochastic model is different, so one run per value of `beta`
says little. `n_particles` sets the number of realisations to run for each
parameter set:

```{r}
pars <- data.frame(beta = c(0.2, 0.3, 0.5))
res <- run_parameter_sets(sir, pars, times = 0:100,
                          fixed = list(gamma = 0.1), n_particles = 100,
                          dt = 0.25)

beta <- dplyr::select(tidy_pars(res), sample, beta = value)
traj <- dplyr::left_join(tidy_trajectories(res, vars = "I"), beta,
                         by = "sample")
traj
```

There is now a `particle` column, with 100 realisations for each value of
`beta`:

```{r}
ggplot(traj, aes(time, value, colour = factor(beta),
                 group = interaction(beta, particle))) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.15) +
  scale_colour_met_d("Hokusai2") +
  labs(y = "I", colour = "beta") +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(override.aes = list(alpha = 1)))
```

`summarise_trajectories()` summarises over particles and draws, keeping any
other columns as groups. Because `beta` has been joined on, the summary is
per value of `beta`:

```{r}
ggplot(summarise_trajectories(traj),
       aes(time, fill = factor(beta), colour = factor(beta))) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lower, ymax = upper), alpha = 0.3, colour = NA) +
  geom_line(aes(y = median)) +
  scale_colour_met_d("Hokusai2") +
  scale_fill_met_d("Hokusai2") +
  labs(y = "I", fill = "beta", colour = "beta")
```

A stochastic model can also be run without the noise, by passing
`deterministic = TRUE`. Random draws are then replaced by their
expectations and there is a single trajectory per parameter set.

## Running from monty output

The draws from a fit are another collection of parameter sets. Fit the
stochastic model to some case data with a particle filter, saving the
trajectories and the final state of each sample:

```{r}
data <- data.frame(
  time = 1:20,
  cases = c(4, 8, 5, 12, 13, 19, 29, 34, 39, 42, 51, 44, 49, 38, 41, 33, 27,
            21, 22, 13))
filter <- dust_filter_create(sir, time_start = 0, data = data,
                             n_particles = 100, dt = 0.25)
packer <- monty_packer(c("beta", "gamma"), fixed = list(N = 1000, I0 = 10))
likelihood <- dust_likelihood_monty(filter, packer, save_trajectories = TRUE,
                                    save_state = TRUE)
prior <- monty_dsl({
  beta ~ Exponential(mean = 0.5)
  gamma ~ Exponential(mean = 0.2)
})
vcv <- matrix(c(0.051, 0.040, 0.040, 0.035), 2, 2)
sampler <- monty_sampler_random_walk(vcv)
samples <- monty_sample(likelihood + prior, sampler, 3000,
                        initial = c(0.7, 0.45), n_chains = 3)
samples <- monty_samples_thin(samples, burnin = 1000, thinning_factor = 5)

fit <- tidy_trajectories(samples, filter, vars = "incidence")
```

```{r}
cols <- met.brewer("Demuth", 5)
cols_scenario <- c("fit" = cols[5], "baseline" = cols[5],
                   "projection" =  cols[4],
                  "30% lower transmission" = cols[1])
```

### Continuing a fit

`continue_parameter_sets()` carries on from the final state and time of a
set of samples, with each sample continuing from its own state using its
own parameters. The model, its time step and the time of the last data
point are taken from the filter, and the packer says how to turn each
sample into parameters for the model. This needs the final state, so the
likelihood must have been created with `save_state = TRUE`.

Here each posterior sample is projected forward 20 days:

```{r}
projection <- continue_parameter_sets(samples, times = 20:40, obj = filter,
                                      packer = packer)

both <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  fit = fit,
  projection = tidy_trajectories(projection, vars = "incidence"),
  .id = "period")

ggplot(both, aes(time, value)) +
  geom_line(aes(group = interaction(sample, period), colour = period),
            alpha = 0.03) +
  geom_point(aes(y = cases), data = data) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = cols_scenario) +
  labs(y = "incidence") +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(override.aes = list(alpha = 1)))
```

The result can itself be continued, and `n_particles` runs several
realisations forward from each sample's state.

### Counterfactuals

A counterfactual reruns the model with some parameters changed. Convert
the samples to a data frame with one row per sample, and change the
parameters there:

```{r}
pars <- posterior::as_draws_df(samples)
pars

pars_reduced <- pars
pars_reduced$beta <- pars$beta * 0.7
```

Then run both sets from the start. Passing the filter in place of the model
means the time step and start time match the fit:

```{r}
baseline <- run_parameter_sets(filter, pars, times = 0:40, packer = packer)
reduced <- run_parameter_sets(filter, pars_reduced, times = 0:40,
                              packer = packer)
```

The baseline is rerun rather than taken from the fit so that the comparison
is like for like: trajectories saved during a fit have been filtered
towards the data, whereas these are both free simulations.

```{r}
scenarios <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  baseline = tidy_trajectories(baseline, vars = "incidence"),
  "30% lower transmission" = tidy_trajectories(reduced, vars = "incidence"),
  .id = "scenario")
scenarios$scenario <- factor(scenarios$scenario, unique(scenarios$scenario))

ggplot(summarise_trajectories(scenarios), aes(time, fill = scenario)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lower, ymax = upper), alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_line(aes(y = median, colour = scenario)) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = cols_scenario, aesthetics = c("fill", "colour")) +
  labs(y = "incidence")
```

The same changed parameters can be used from the end of the fit instead,
for an intervention that starts on day 20. Each sample still continues from
its own fitted state:

```{r}
intervention <- continue_parameter_sets(samples, times = 20:40, obj = filter,
                                        packer = packer, pars = pars_reduced)

future <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  fit = fit,
  baseline = tidy_trajectories(projection, vars = "incidence"),
  "30% lower transmission" = tidy_trajectories(intervention,
                                                vars = "incidence"),
  .id = "scenario")
future$scenario <- factor(future$scenario, unique(future$scenario))

ggplot(summarise_trajectories(future), aes(time, fill = scenario)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lower, ymax = upper), alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_line(aes(y = median, colour = scenario)) +
  geom_point(aes(time, cases), data = data, inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = cols_scenario, aesthetics = c("fill", "colour")) +
  labs(y = "incidence")
```

Parameters that are fixed in the packer, such as `N` here, can be changed
for a counterfactual with the `fixed` argument of either function.
